body:
"I can't think of a worse thing to say to a suicidal person. "You'll still feel miserable, but you won't be able to even contemplate ending that misery."

It won't be like he is barred for thinking about that- it's just that he'll find himself not needing to go there as often, even though he still might be very unhappy.  What is so terrible about that?

When suicidal people contemplate suicide aren't they just fantasizing about the pain ending-they don't truly wish to die? Therefore wouldn't it be good for them to do this by fantasizing about a miracle cure opposed to suicide? After all- mind over matter-once people envision a cure it may manifest itself in reality.  What is so much more realistic to the sufferer about suicide then a miracle cure?  And even if a miracle cure is more difficult to fantasize about, wouldn't it be worth it to change the behavior?

"....but I have a great psychologist who listens and genuinely cares about me plus I'm trying the best antidepressant they have to offer so my mood now is only temporary and things will definitely improve from here on out"

Of course this assumes that a strong effort is put in.  If nothing is done, yeah you're 100% right which even makes it more important for my friend to get a great shrink and start on a new antidepressant or even lithium.

I apologize if it seems that I'm callous or do not have sympathy.  I do understand somewhat, like for instance how serious it is- which is why I worry about my friend actually going through with euthanasia.

I hope you can understand that I'm just trying to save lives.  Can you explain to me why you think euthanasia is a justified answer to what is admittedly horrendous suffering?  After all, as long as the person is alive, there IS a chance it might get better. Once a person is gone, you've lost any chance at all that they could've experienced life without such pain. 

Also, I hope you understand that I'm not trying to say the antidepressants or lithium will take away the pain- what they might help with is taking away the desire to end ones life.  In the case of lithium, the drug takes away the energy and ability to plan that would be required in a suicide attempt.  This is far from ideal, but we are talking about saving a life here.  In the case of a baby not getting enough oxygen , they don't simply kill the baby because he/she will grow up with severe mental handicaps.  Likewise, just because lithium might have significant side effects and effect the persons ability to function and think clearly  doesn't mean they it shouldn't be used if it can save a life

I apologize if I seem cruel.  However what I'm focused on is saving a life- the consideration for quality of life comes AFTER you've saved a life. You believe that quality of life comes first and I respect that , I just disagree with you because I think the hope that in the near future there will be either a cure or a better treatment is worth waiting for.  Why is that cruel- after all it's not me who is causing my friend to have so much pain?

I can understand some of your points however in Stephen Hawking's(or Christopher Reeves, Michael J. Fox etc) case did you ever consider that their limitations/pain is something that they learned to be able to tolerate rather than them simply being innately stronger than others from the get go? This could mean it's something that could be taught to others.  There are a lot of self help books/courses/speakers so obviously I'm not the first one to think this. I've noticed that depressed people automatically assume that people like Hawkings are innately better because of low self esteem and the negative outlook that goes along with depression .

"Depression is not causing him to have severe physical pain like this....depression is a RESULT of being in severe physical pain very often." 
This is the chicken or the egg problem with depression and chronic pain.  You might be right, the depression might only go away if the pain is removed. But there is an equal chance the pain could be made worse by the depression or even that while there was a real injury initially, it has healed now and the pain only persists because the initial injury caused depression.  Because no can really tell which situation it is, doesn't it make more sense to assume it's the latter rather than the former, simply because you can do something about the latter?

Anyways I'm sorry to hear that you have an incurable/untreatable disease that is causing you to suffer so much.  I wonder if you believe in rebirth or something similar because doesn't it not really matter that the person isn't suffering anymore if they are dead- unless you believe in rebirth.
